items.desc: SpaceX brought back its Starship rocket's second stage today for a first-ever midair capture at its launch pad, capping a record-setting orbital flight test.

items.title: Flat optics roadmap charts path toward smaller imaging and sensing systems
items.desc: For centuries, optical systems have relied on lenses, mirrors and other components that manipulate light through their shape and size. Today, advances in nanotechnology are enabling a different approach. Researchers can now engineer materials at scales smaller than the wavelength of light, creating ultrathin optical components that offer new ways to control how light behaves.

items.title: Early black holes may have grown through productive chaos
items.desc: When the universe was less than 700 million years old, the supermassive black hole powering a quasar called J0313-1806 had already grown to about 3 billion times the mass of the sun. It is one of the most extreme examples of a puzzle that has occupied astrophysicists for two decades: How did supermassive black holes grow so big so quickly?

items.title: 'Buffer spaces' may help resolve workplace concerns
items.desc: Nearly every person will run into conflict in their workplace at some point in their career, but it can be difficult to know when or how to report these concerns.

items.title: AI could help speed up research ethics approvals
items.desc: Artificial intelligence programs could be used to improve efficiency for professionals dealing with research ethics reviews, enabling humans to focus on the ethical decision-making.

items.title: Flip side: Upside-down atomic layers could steer heat in stacked computer chips
items.desc: Stacking chips on top of one another could keep computers getting faster, but it creates a heating problem. Now, researchers from Japan have found that simply flipping atom-thin layers upside down could help steer that heat where it needs to go.

items.title: New analysis shows that even young children want to be seen as morally good
items.desc: As early as 130,000 years ago, the first human societies were built on morality and cooperation within groups. The same is true today. Even young children exhibit a distinctly human desire to be seen as morally good. That is the conclusion of a new article by researchers at Leipzig University. Humboldt Research Fellow Dr. Leon Li and Junior Professor Dr. Sebastian Grüneisen are investigating the origins of human cooperation and social identity. Their paper, "Evolutionary foundations of social identity," has just been published in the journal Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: B

items.title: Tigers, zebras, quantum dots: Nanoparticles assemble into patterns
items.desc: Forget about how the zebra got its stripes. For a group of Cornell engineers, an equally important question is: What drives the formation of such eye-catching patterns?

items.title: Capping nanovials that trap cells and their secretions for analysis enables new bioscience experiments
items.desc: A UCLA-developed technology that is like a test tube but on the cellular scale has led to a number of biomedical discoveries in recent years, including revelations about cancer, heart disease and the genetic levers that push cells to release proteins.

items.title: Researchers are testing whether agrivoltaics can help farmers adapt to hotter, drier conditions
items.desc: Majdi Abou Najm stands in a tomato crop under the summer sun in UC Davis' agricultural research fields. A few hours after sunrise, the sun is beginning to feel less like warmth and more like a weight—the kind of heat that could scald tomatoes on the vine.

items.title: Euclid's H-alpha observations map where stars form in distant galaxies
items.desc: Euclid was launched into space in July 2023 to explore two of astronomy's biggest mysteries: dark matter and dark energy. The space telescope's first major data release covers some 1,900 square degrees of the sky, equivalent to around 14% of the area planned for the six-year mission and around 5% of the total sky. It is an unprecedented collection of visible and near-infrared observations.

items.title: Long-term study reveals how humidity affects the durability of biodegradable thermoplastic polymers
items.desc: As the demand for sustainable alternatives to conventional plastics continues to grow, biodegradable polymers such as poly(lactic acid) (PLA) are attracting increasing attention for applications ranging from packaging to consumer products.

items.title: Tiny switch harnesses four electrical states, moving beyond simple on-off control
items.desc: From light switches to transistors, many kinds of switches have exactly two states: on or off, conducting or insulating, zero or one. Researchers at TU Wien are working with unusual materials that challenge some of the standard assumptions of materials physics. Using one of these materials, they have developed a tiny switch with four distinct states and several ways to move between them. This opens up new ways to process and store information. The study is published in the journal Communications Materials.

items.title: Turning biomass into renewable fuels and chemicals using microorganisms
items.desc: Texas A&M University researchers have developed a process that converts biomass into renewable fuels and chemicals. Dr. Mark Holtzapple, professor in the Artie McFerrin Department of Chemical Engineering, aims to make producing these products more efficient and affordable by using microorganisms to break down plant material.

items.title: AI tool counts mosquito eggs in smartphone photos to aid surveillance
items.desc: Your mission, should you choose to accept it: Track down and identify thousands of nearly microscopic mosquito eggs hiding in plain sight. Your only weapon? A smartphone armed with artificial intelligence.

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
items.desc: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.

items.title: The secret to building Moon bases may be hiding in emergency blankets
items.desc: Scientists have turned the thin plastic used in emergency blankets into remarkably strong insulation that could help astronauts survive the Moon's extreme temperatures. Built from hundreds of stacked layers, the material withstands crushing pressure without losing its thermal protection, potentially paving the way for tougher, longer-lasting lunar habitats.

items.title: NASA is offering $1 million for bold ideas to help build a Moon base
items.desc: NASA is offering $1 million in its new Moon Base Challenge, inviting U.S. students to develop innovative solutions for building humanity’s first permanent lunar outpost. From power systems to astronaut safety, their ideas could help make long-term life on the Moon possible and pave the way to Mars.

items.title: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain
items.desc: New research reveals that biological sex, genetics, and menopause may dramatically influence Alzheimer's risk, treatment responses, and chronic pain conditions such as fibromyalgia. Scientists also uncovered surprising differences in immune activity and gut-brain interactions, opening the door to more personalized treatments for neurological disorders.

items.title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.

items.title: Physicists defy expectations by controlling the magnetic heart of a single atom
items.desc: Scientists have unexpectedly discovered how to control the magnetic spin inside a single atom's nucleus using radio waves, overturning previous assumptions about atomic behavior. The breakthrough could pave the way for more reliable quantum memory, although researchers are still trying to understand why it works.

items.title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
items.desc: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

items.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
items.desc: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields. Remarkably, the models indicate that their magnetic poles could shift by tens of degrees within just a few decades, far faster than Earth's.

items.title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
items.desc: Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

items.title: Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock
items.desc: Deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have discovered tiny hidden ecosystems inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. Researchers examined 244 nodules and found more than 4,100 animals living in their cracks and cavities, including unique communities unlike those in the surrounding seafloor mud. These remarkable miniature habitats could now be threatened by deep-sea mining for valuable metals.

items.title: Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
items.desc: Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

items.title: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
items.desc: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.

items.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
items.desc: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice. Even more remarkably, giving mice arginine after they contracted influenza helped them recover.

items.title: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression
items.desc: A simple change to your daily routine could make a surprising difference in how you feel, both physically and mentally. University of Missouri researchers found that older adults who followed consistent daily schedules reported less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggled with insomnia. Keeping regular times for sleeping, eating, and other activities may help regulate the body's internal clock, which influences mood, sleep, and overall health.

items.title: Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns
items.desc: ESA’s Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 ancient quasars, including two record-breaking objects that shone with the brightness of a trillion Suns when the Universe was just 670 million years old. Powered by supermassive black holes, these extraordinary cosmic beacons reveal a time when the first galaxies were still taking shape.

items.title: America After the Midterms
items.desc: The Democrats came out on top in the midterms by staying on message and focusing on affordability. But from voters’ perspective, there is an enormous difference between repudiating the administration and embracing the alternative.

items.title: Can Brexit Be Reversed?
items.desc: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Brexit a mistake, and opinion polls show that his proposal to "go all the way" and rejoin the European Union has majority support. But Brexit was won by a movement, and only a movement can reverse it.

items.title: Portfolio Regime Change?
items.desc: Rather than assuming that traditional asset-allocation guidelines apply to current conditions, investors should position themselves for more volatility and uncertainty. The AI revolution and various structural forces mean that there is no going back to the familiar old diversification formula.

items.title: The Global Economy After the Iran War Ends
items.desc: Even if the Iran war ended tomorrow, the global economy would not simply pick up where it left off. Reopening the Strait of Hormuz could bring down commodity prices and ease inflation, but postwar reconstruction could redirect capital away from the United States, undermining the AI supercycle and fueling de-dollarization.

items.title: Breaking Billionaires’ Political Grip
items.desc: The US midterm elections showed that despite the outsize role of money in politics, even the biggest donors don’t always get their way. But defeating billionaires at the ballot box won’t stop them from buying political influence as long as the rules permit them to do so.

items.title: The Dance of Empires
items.desc: Empires have a habit of preparing to fight the last war while their rivals work out how to win the next one. The US is no different, pouring its resources into military adventures while China slowly but steadily reclaims the scientific and technological leadership that once made it the world's greatest power.

items.title: The Rare-Earth Game
items.desc: China will probably not impose a rare-earth embargo, but it will keep the specter of one alive. And the West will probably not achieve self-sufficiency in this critical sector, but it will keep seeking to reduce its vulnerability to a supply shock through expensive capacity duplication and stockpiles.

items.title: Why Research Matters
items.desc: Over the past 21 months, in the country that has leveraged research to greatest effect, the government is slashing funding for it, closing centers where it is done, politicizing grant-making decisions, and bullying its single biggest engine: universities. The costs will be far greater than many realize.

items.title: Africa Needs a Different Kind of Climate Finance
items.desc: Roughly half of the climate finance that flows to Africa comes in the form of debt, with multilateral and bilateral development-finance institutions often lending at commercial rates to economies already struggling to carry the added costs. To maximize fiscal space, the instruments used to deliver climate finance need to change.

items.title: Effective Climate Action Requires Capable States
items.desc: With delegations from around the world gathering for another international climate conference, the question today is not whether governments should do more to address the climate crisis, but whether they even have the capabilities to do so. After 40 years of free-market orthodoxy, many simply do not.

items.title: Why Is Mexico Defying Latin America’s Right Turn?
items.desc: How Mexico’s left has managed to retain strong support is a key question of contemporary Latin American politics. The most likely answer centers on the ruling Morena party’s pragmatic brand of left-wing politics, which combines bold redistributive policies, greater security, and a willingness to compromise in the name of both.

items.title: The Digital-Currency Divide
items.desc: The rush to develop central bank digital currencies has slowed as underwhelming demand and mounting costs have given governments second thoughts. But while the Federal Reserve and other central banks have shelved their plans, the European Central Bank is pressing ahead with its digital euro.

items.title: The ASEAN Paradox
items.desc: As the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gathers for its 49th Summit, several rifts have exposed the group’s institutional shortcomings. But amid a fracturing global order, ASEAN must choose: turn its convening authority into concerted action or be reduced to an arena for great-power rivalry.

items.title: Medical AI Needs Bedside Manners
items.desc: Even the most accurate medical AI tools have little value if they make patients uneasy or doctors find them too cumbersome. A comfort-by-design approach could overcome these obstacles by involving patients and practitioners in development and ensuring that new systems work with existing medical practices.

items.title: Reviving the Legacy of Reykjavík
items.desc: As nuclear threats grow, AI accelerates, and international law comes under strain, the world urgently needs a renewed commitment to dialogue. Today's leaders can find a template in the landmark 1986 summit between then US President Ronald Reagan and Soviet President Mikhail Gorbachev.
